title: The Hanging
subtitle: Monday 19 to Saturday 24 April 1886: A Sign on a Dead Man, a Widow's Coffee Can, Guns on the Rawlins Stage

setting.name: Gilead and the middle creek, the week of the hanging
setting.description: The week Owen Lasker is found hanged at the Narrows. The party arrives in Gilead on Monday noon, is offered work by three factions and a widow, and has six days to look at the body, the tree, the tracks and the town before the valley chooses sides for good. On Tuesday Dr. Abigail Haskell holds the inquest in the courthouse. On Wednesday Owen is buried on the bluff above the Narrows. On Friday eight hired gunmen from Cheyenne step off the Rawlins stage. On Saturday night the grange meets at Solberg's Bend to vote on whether to arm. The sandbox is Gilead's one street, the eleven-mile road up the creek to the Narrows, Solberg's Bend between them, and, for a party hired by the Company, the long ride up to the Forks. Every clue the party needs to know that the Association did not do this is in the first two days, in plain sight, for anyone who looks at the sign instead of the dead man.
setting.atmosphere: Mud and meltwater. The creek is bank-full and brown and loud; the road is a pair of ruts in black gumbo that sucks the shoes off horses; the snow is going grey in the draws and the first green is coming on the south slopes. The sky is enormous and changes every hour, sun, then a squall of sleet, then sun. In town, everyone is talking and nobody is saying anything. Men stand on opposite sides of the street. The Plainsman's bulletin board has a crowd round it all day. Somebody has chalked STROUD on the Company's office door and somebody else has rubbed it off. At the Narrows, the cottonwood is a hundred years old and the rope is still on the limb because nobody wants to be the one to take it down.

keyLocations.name: The Narrows: the cottonwood and the Lasker cabin
keyLocations.description: Eleven miles up the creek from Gilead, the valley pinches between two red sandstone bluffs, and the creek runs fast and shallow over gravel: the best ford for twenty miles, and a natural place for a dam. A huge old cottonwood leans over the ford on the near bank. Fifty yards up the slope is Owen and Thea Lasker's one-room log cabin, a lean-to stable, a root cellar, a potato patch fenced with wire, nine head of cattle and a milk cow. Thea found Owen at first light on Monday; the neighbours cut him down at eight and laid him in the cabin, and the rope is still on the limb.
features: The cottonwood: a limb twelve feet up, the bark scraped raw where the rope ran over it; the end of the rope tied off round the trunk with a clumsy granny knot, not a cowhand's hitch
The sign, now on the cabin table under a tin cup: a sheet of heavy printed paper, lettered on the back in black ink
The ford's mud and the road bank: a mess of tracks from the neighbours on Monday morning, but older tracks underneath along the upstream bank, where no one has walked

The cabin: a stove, a bed, a table, a shelf of books, a family Bible, a coffee can on the shelf above the stove, and, nailed on the inside of the door where Thea moved it so the boy would not read it, a square of cartridge-box card
encounters: Thea Lasker, the widow, and her six-year-old son Pete, with two neighbour women sitting with the body
Nils Solberg and three young homesteaders, armed, who ride in on Monday afternoon wanting to go up to the Forks and kill somebody tonight
secrets: CLUE A1 (core, automatic for anyone who turns the sign over or looks at it with care): the sign reads RUSTLER. THE ASSOCIATION GIVES FAIR WARNING in neat, even copperplate, black iron-gall ink, a clerk's hand with flourished capitals. It is lettered on the blank back of a printed General Land Office form; the printed side, turned over, is headed with the Land Office's name and has spaces for an entry number and a quarter-section. Investigation DC 12 notices that it has been carefully trimmed to remove the form's title line. Anyone who has filed a homestead claim (Clara Solberg, Calvin Booker, Gustav Lindahl) recognises the paper at once.

CLUE A2 (core, automatic for anyone who looks at the inside of the door): the square of cartridge-box card reads, in heavy, ill-spelled pencil capitals, LASKER YOU ARE WARND OUT. 30 DAYS. P.R.S.G.A. 5 APRIL. This is Jubal Stroud's real Association warning. The thirty days had not run. Nobody in the valley has ever seen Stroud letter anything neatly.

CLUE A3 (core for a Scout's Trailcraft or anyone who searches the upstream bank; Survival DC 13 otherwise): beneath the Monday mess, two shod horses came down the creek road from the direction of Gilead on Sunday night, stood under the cottonwood, and went back the way they came at a lope. One of them wears a bar shoe on the near fore, a shoe with a bar across the heel, put on for a cracked hoof. Survival DC 16: they were not cow ponies from the Forks, which go unshod in the off-season; these were town-shod horses. Nobody came down from the upper valley.

CLUE C4 (Thea will give it only when she trusts the party: Insight DC 14 to see that she is hiding something, then honesty, kindness or a promise to find the truth rather than a culprit): in the family Bible, at the Book of Ruth, a page torn from Owen's survey notebook in his small hand: 'G.S. is the one giving names. Saw the letter on his desk, Cheyenne, $75. Told him Fri. Will say it at grange Sat. 24th.' Thea does not know who G.S. is; Owen would not tell her, 'so you can say you never knew.' She suspects it means Gideon Sayre and is afraid to say so to anyone in the grange, because Sayre is the grange's secretary.

CLUE E2 and E3 (in the coffee can, with $112 in notes and coins, Thea's savings): Owen's draft of a letter to 'Mr. H. Wendt, Chief Engineer', offering to sell the Narrows to the railroad on condition that any dam leave 'a fair head of water for the ditches below, my neighbours' living depends on it'; and a Company letter from February, signed C. Ballantine, offering $1,500 for the quarter and its water right, which Owen refused. The Ballantine letter makes the Company look guilty.

keyLocations.name: Gilead's Main Street: the Plainsman, the courthouse, Greaves Mercantile and the smithy
keyLocations.description: Gilead's one long street runs from the creek bridge to the stage barn, with plank walks in front of the better buildings and mud everywhere else. The Plainsman office has a hand press, a cat and Lavinia Thorpe, who is setting a special edition by hand. The two-storey Ransom County courthouse holds the sheriff's office, the jail, the clerk and the commissioners' room, where the inquest sits on Tuesday. Greaves Mercantile sells everything from coffee to coffins, and Otis Greaves keeps a credit ledger in which half the valley owes him money. Moses Kearney's livery and smithy is at the stage barn end, where the ring of the hammer starts at six.
features: The Plainsman's window bulletin, updated by Lavinia Thorpe in chalk as news comes in, and the files of every issue since 1884, bound, on a shelf
Greaves Mercantile's rope: coils of manila on a peg behind the counter, 3/4-inch, at four cents a foot, and the credit ledger under the counter
The smithy's account slate and Moses Kearney's memory for every hoof in the county
Sheriff Quinlan's office: a stove, a gun rack, a spittoon, two iron cells and a desk drawer full of IOUs and unanswered letters
encounters: The crowd outside the Plainsman: grangers on one side of the street, Company cowboys on the other; a fist fight starts at three on Monday if nobody stops it (two Saloon Brawlers and a Drunk Cowboy against three angry homesteaders)
Sheriff Silas Quinlan, trying to be everywhere and agree with everyone
secrets: CLUE B2 (core for anyone who asks Greaves about rope, or reads his ledger; Persuasion DC 12 to get a look at the ledger, automatic if Beau Fairchild asks, because Greaves owes him a favour): on Saturday 17 April, forty feet of new 3/4-inch manila, $1.60, sold to Ira Pettit, paid in cash. Greaves remembers it because Pettit already owes the store $11 and did not pay a cent of that. 'Said it was for a corral. He hasn't got a corral.'

CLUE B1 (core for anyone who asks the smith about the bar shoe): Moses Kearney put a bar shoe on Elam Henley's bay gelding's near fore in March, for a quarter crack. 'Only bar shoe I've set this year. Henley still owes me for it.' On Tuesday he will add that Henley paid it, and the six dollars before it, on Monday afternoon, in a new five and a one.

CLUE C1 (detail, needs a comparison): any filing on display at the courthouse, any notarised paper, the grange's minute book or the notice of the grange meeting in the Plainsman's window, all written by Gideon Sayre, show the same neat copperplate and black iron-gall ink as the sign. The party must think to compare them; Investigation DC 13 makes the match certain once they do.

Lavinia Thorpe has received, by Saturday's mail from Cheyenne, an anonymous copy of the Association's dead list: ten names, one struck through. She does not know whether to print it. Printing it will bring the war faster; not printing it will leave nine living men on it who do not know. She will ask the party what they would do.

keyLocations.name: Gideon Sayre's office
keyLocations.description: A neat clapboard office beside the courthouse with a gilt-lettered window: G. SAYRE, LAND LOCATOR. NOTARY PUBLIC. U.S. COMMISSIONER. Inside, a counter, a big township plat map of the valley on the wall with every claim pencilled in and numbered, a roll-top desk, a letter press, a locked iron safe, and pigeonholes of printed General Land Office blanks: homestead applications, affidavits, final proofs, relinquishments. Sayre is here from eight to six, and he is charming, helpful, grave, and the most useful man in town to anyone who wants to know who owns what.
features: The plat map: the Narrows quarter is pencilled 'Lasker' with a fresh line through it, and on Tuesday afternoon a new name is written in: 'Henley'
The commissioner's register, a big ledger on the counter in which every filing and proof he takes is entered by date
The pigeonholes of blank forms, one of them half empty
The safe, which holds his letter book, the Association's letters and the money
encounters: Gideon Sayre, who will help the party with anything: maps, names, who owns which quarter, his own opinion that 'the Company has gone too far this time'
On Tuesday afternoon, Elam Henley, filing a homestead entry with a grin
secrets: Sayre will volunteer to the party, sorrowfully, that 'poor Owen relinquished his claim to me only a week before; said he was giving up and going back to Iowa; I have the paper here.' He shows a relinquishment dated 10 April, Owen's name signed, witnessed by E. Henley and I. Pettit. This is the forgery. It is more than a lie: it is the only reason Sayre talks about it, because he needs the town to know the claim was relinquished before the widow thinks to contest it.

CLUE B5 (from Tuesday 20 April, core for anyone who reads the register): 'No. 1186. 20 April 1886. Homestead entry, Elam Henley, NE quarter, Sec. 14 (the Narrows), on relinquishment of O. Lasker.' Sayre mails it to Cheyenne on Thursday's stage.

If anyone tells Sayre what they have found (the sign's paper, the bar shoe, the rope), he thanks them, says he will see the sheriff about it, and sends Henley and Pettit out of town to 'look for work at the roundup'. He also writes to the Association that 'certain strangers are making inquiries', which puts the party on Stroud's attention.

Sleight of Hand or Stealth DC 15 at night (the window latch is cheap) gets inside; Mechanics DC 17 opens the safe. Inside: the Association secretary's letters thanking 'G.S.' for names, with receipts for $25 a name going back to 1884 (a version of CLUE C3), and $1,140 in notes. Breaking in is a crime; anything taken this way is evidence the judge will not admit in bk-scenario-004 unless someone else finds it there lawfully.

keyLocations.name: The Antelope Saloon
keyLocations.description: The best building in Gilead after the courthouse: a forty-foot bar of real walnut freighted from Omaha, a mirror, a piano with eleven working keys, a faro layout, two poker tables and a back room. Owned two-thirds by Rufus Kemble, a fat, cheerful former freighter, and one-third since March by Beaumont Fairchild, who won it at cards. The Company's cowboys drink here; homesteaders, mostly, do not. On Monday night it is full and loud and everyone is armed.
features: The back room's poker table, where Sheriff Quinlan has lost $400 since Christmas, most of it to Beau Fairchild
Kemble's slate of who owes the house what
The front window, which looks across the street at Sayre's office
encounters: Company cowboys drinking to the hanging and some drinking against it; a Drunk Cowboy picks a fight with any homesteader or stranger who comes in
Elam Henley and Ira Pettit, at a corner table on Monday night, Henley buying drinks and Pettit not drinking his
secrets: CLUE B3 (core for anyone who asks Kemble about debts, or for Beau Fairchild, who sees the slate): on Monday afternoon both Henley and Pettit paid off their slates, $38 and $27, in new banknotes, and Henley bought a round for the house. Neither has had work since February.

Insight DC 13 on Ira Pettit: he is not drunk; he is sick, and every time someone at the bar says 'Lasker' he looks at the door. If anyone sits with him and is gentle (Gustav Lindahl has advantage), he says one thing before Henley pulls him away: 'You ever see a man... no. Nothing. Forget it.'
Henley carries a new Army revolver he could not afford in March.

keyLocations.name: The Forks: the BC Home Ranch
keyLocations.description: Twenty-eight miles up the valley, a long day's ride from Gilead: the Company's big log house with its glassed veranda, three bunkhouses, a cookhouse, the blacksmith shop and the horse corrals, where in April the cowboys are breaking the remuda's green horses for the roundup. Cyrus Ballantine keeps his office in the house; Wade Tolliver keeps his in the corral.
features: The breaking corral, dust and shouting and a bronc going up in the air every quarter hour
The cookhouse and the roundup cook's tally book of who ate which meals
Ballantine's office: a desk, a safe, a telegraph-form pad and a framed share certificate of the Bitter Creek Land & Cattle Company, Limited
encounters: Cyrus Ballantine, courteous and cold, who regrets the death and does not regret its effect
Wade Tolliver, the range boss, who is angry about the hanging for reasons of his own
Jubal Stroud, if he is at the ranch, cleaning a rifle on the veranda
secrets: CLUE A4 (core for anyone who asks where the Company's men were on Sunday night): every one of the thirty-one riders at the Forks was in the bunkhouses, after a day breaking horses, and the cook fed thirty-one at breakfast at four on Monday; Tolliver had the night guard on the horse herd and counted them. Wade Tolliver: 'I don't hang men. And if I did, I'd use a riata, not storebought rope, and I'd tie it so it held.'

Ballantine is glad Owen is dead and does not hide it from people he thinks are on his side. He sent the telegram for the gunmen for the gunmen on Monday night (it went down by rider to Rawlins). He has not ordered anyone hanged, ever, and is faintly insulted at the suggestion that he would do it so crudely.
Wade Tolliver fired Henley and Pettit in February for drinking on night guard. He knows Henley's bay with the bar shoe.

synopsis: The party rides into Gilead on Monday 19 April, the day Owen Lasker is found hanged at the Narrows, and is offered work: by the Company as range inspectors, by the grange as protection, by the sheriff as deputies, or by the widow, Thea Lasker, with $112 in a coffee can. Whoever hires them, the scenario asks them to look at a hanging that every faction has already explained. At the Narrows, the sign is lettered in a clerk's copperplate on the back of a Land Office form, Stroud's real thirty-day warning is still on the cabin door, and two town-shod horses, one wearing a bar shoe, came from Gilead and went back to it. In town, the smith shod Henley's bay with a bar shoe, Greaves sold Ira Pettit forty feet of rope on Saturday, and both drifters paid their debts on Monday in new banknotes. Gideon Sayre, the helpful notary, produces a relinquishment that says Owen gave up his claim a week before he died, and on Tuesday records Elam Henley's new entry on the Narrows. Meanwhile the war gathers: an inquest returns 'persons unknown', the funeral turns into a political meeting, Nils Solberg wants blood, eight hired guns arrive on Friday's stage, Stroud nails new warnings on two more doors, Ballantine offers the widow $300, and on Saturday night the grange votes on whether to arm. By the end of the week the party should know that the Association did not hang Owen Lasker and that two drifters did, and should have a thread, the paper and the handwriting, leading toward the man who paid them. What they do with that, and whom they tell, is the first of the campaign's choices.
hook: Monday noon, Gilead, in front of the Plainsman's window: the news from the Narrows, a street split down the middle, and four offers of work in a quarter of an hour. Thea Lasker, who rode in on the boy's mule behind him, waits until the others have finished, then says only this: 'They'll tell you it was the Company. Maybe it was. I want to know, not be told. I have a hundred and twelve dollars.'

conclusions.conclusion: A. The hanging was not the Association's or the Company's work
clues: A1: the sign, copperplate on the back of a Land Office blank (the Narrows)
A2: Stroud's real thirty-day card on the cabin door (the Narrows)
A3: the tracks came from and went back to Gilead (the Narrows)
A4: every Company rider was at the Forks (the Forks, the cook, Tolliver)
A5: Stroud's own word (the road, Friday)

conclusions.conclusion: B. Elam Henley and Ira Pettit did the hanging
clues: B1: the bar shoe on Henley's bay (the smithy)
B2: Pettit bought forty feet of rope on Saturday (Greaves Mercantile)
B3: both paid their debts on Monday in new banknotes (the Antelope, the smithy)
B5: Henley filed on the Narrows on Tuesday (Sayre's register)

conclusions.conclusion: D. The Company means to clear the creek
clues: D1: Stroud's cards on Booker's door and two more, and Lavinia Thorpe's copy of the dead list (the creek, the Plainsman)
D2: eight gunmen with Association commissions on Friday's stage (Gilead)
E3: Ballantine's offers for the Narrows (the coffee can, Saturday)
Ballantine's own words to anyone he thinks is his (the Forks)

acts.title: Monday: The Crowd and the Cottonwood
acts.description: The party arrives, is hired, and rides to the Narrows. The point of this act is to establish the valley's factions in a single street and then put the party under the cottonwood while the evidence is fresh. A party that takes the Company's money can still ride to the Narrows: Ballantine's office manager will want to know 'what the grangers are saying'. Let the players argue about whose money to take; whoever hires them, Thea is at the cabin and the sign is on her table.
objectives: Choose an employer, or several, and agree terms
Ride to the Narrows and examine the tree, the sign, the tracks and the cabin
Keep Nils Solberg and his friends from riding on the Forks tonight
Earn enough of Thea Lasker's trust to be told what Owen knew

scenes.name: Four Offers
scenes.description: The crowd outside the Plainsman. Run the hiring as a quick, sharp scene with four voices. The Company's office manager in Gilead, a dry Scots bookkeeper named Duncan Lyall, offers range inspectors' wages, $60 a month and found, Association commissions, and a $5 bonus for 'every head of stolen stock recovered'. Margit Solberg, Worthy Master of the grange, offers $20 a month a head from a subscription, meals at any table on the creek, and her hand on it. Sheriff Silas Quinlan offers special deputies' badges at $3 a day, county scrip, 'payable when the commissioners meet'. Thea Lasker offers $112 and says almost nothing. Each pregen's backstory suggests an offer; split loyalties are welcome. Whatever they choose, the street sees it, and the other side remembers. The brawl that starts at three o'clock between three homesteaders and the Company's drinkers is a chance to show what the party is made of in front of the town.
scenes.readAloud: The bulletin in the Plainsman's window is in chalk, in a big round hand: OWEN LASKER OF THE NARROWS FOUND HANGED THIS MORNING. SIGN UPON HIM. SHERIFF NOTIFIED. Under it somebody has written in pencil, STROUD, and somebody else has tried to rub it out. The street is wide and deep in mud, and it has split down the middle as neatly as if someone had drawn a line. On the Antelope's side: big hats, high-heeled boots, spurs, men with their thumbs in their gunbelts saying nothing at all. On the mercantile's side: overalls, brogans, sunbonnets, a woman crying, a red-faced young man shouting that he knows where the Forks is and he has a rifle. Between them, in the mud, the sheriff, a grey stout man with his badge pinned on crooked, keeps turning from one side to the other with his hands up like a man trying to stop two trains. Then they notice you: strangers, armed, with good horses. Within a quarter of an hour, three people have offered you money. The fourth, a thin young woman in a man's coat, with a small boy by the hand and a coffee can under her arm, just looks at you, and waits.

skillChecks.success: You read the four offers. Lyall, the Company's man, is not hiring guns; he is buying witnesses and wants strangers seen on the Company's side. Margit Solberg is frightened for her son more than for the grange. The sheriff is drowning and wants anyone at all between him and the Company and the grange. The widow is the only one who wants to know what happened rather than to be proved right.
skillChecks.failure: Everyone is angry and everyone wants guns; that is all you can tell.

skillChecks.success: You get better terms from whoever you bargain with: the Company adds a month in advance ($60 each); the grange adds a horse apiece on loan; the sheriff pays in cash from his own pocket, not scrip; Thea will not take back her coffee can, but she tells you, quietly, that Owen 'found out something about somebody in town', and that she will show you something at the cabin if you come today.
skillChecks.failure: The terms stand as offered. Whoever you turned down noticed how you did it.

skillChecks.success: When the brawl starts, you stop it with a word and a look, or the threat of a drawn gun; both sides step back and the town sees who did it. Reputation +1. Nils Solberg, shaking, agrees not to ride to the Forks tonight if you go to the Narrows instead.
skillChecks.failure: The brawl happens anyway (two Saloon Brawlers and a Drunk Cowboy against three homesteaders; use brawling rules); someone is going to be hurt unless you wade in.

scenes.name: The Ford
scenes.description: Eleven miles of mud to the Narrows, two to three hours. The neighbours have cut Owen down and laid him out in the cabin; the rope is still on the limb. The tree, the knot and the tracks are here. This is the scene where the mystery is born: let the players look as long as they like. Owen was strangled, not dropped; the GM need say no more than that it was slow and that the neighbours' faces show it. Nils Solberg and three friends ride in during the afternoon, armed, and want to go up to the Forks and 'pay back Stroud'. Stopping them, with words or with evidence that it was not Stroud, is the scene's set piece.
scenes.readAloud: The valley narrows until the red sandstone bluffs on either side are close enough that you can hear the creek's echo off them, and the road comes down to a wide shallow ford where the water runs fast and brown over gravel. Over the ford leans the biggest cottonwood you have seen in the territory, a hundred feet tall, its bark grey and furrowed as an old man's face, its buds just breaking green. From a limb twelve feet up hangs a length of new yellow rope, cut off clean a man's height above the ground, turning a little in the wind. Nobody has taken it down. Fifty yards up the slope is a log cabin with a thread of smoke from its pipe, and two women in black sitting on a bench by the door, and a small boy throwing stones into the creek, hard, one after another, as if he were trying to hit something.

skillChecks.success: Under the trampled Monday mud, along the upstream bank where nobody has walked, two shod horses came down the creek road from the east, from Gilead, on Sunday night after the frost; they stood under the tree a while, and went back the way they came at a lope. One wears a bar shoe on the near fore. Nothing came down from the upper valley. (CLUE A3; automatic for a character with Trailcraft.)
skillChecks.failure: There are a hundred tracks here and the neighbours have walked over all of them. You will need someone who reads sign better, or another look in daylight before more people come.

skillChecks.success: The rope is new manila, three-quarter inch, store-bought, still stiff with sizing; the end is tied off round the trunk with a granny knot that a cowhand would be ashamed of. Cattlemen use rawhide or grass riatas and tie them so they hold. This was done by men who were not used to rope, or were in a hurry, or both.
skillChecks.failure: A rope and a tree. You are not sure what else you expected to see.

skillChecks.success: Nils Solberg listens. If you show him the tracks going back to Gilead, or the sign's paper, he sits down on the bank and weeps for his friend, and then he says, 'Then who?' He will not ride on the Forks tonight. Grange attitude improves by one step.
skillChecks.failure: Nils swears he will ride tonight with or without you. Unless you stop him by force or follow him, the four young men shoot up a Company line camp at midnight and a Company horse is killed; the Company's attitude to the grange, and to any party that was with them, hardens.

scenes.name: The Widow's Cabin
scenes.description: Thea Lasker, twenty-seven, from Iowa, a schoolteacher's daughter who married a man with a claim and a dream; she is not weeping now and will not in front of strangers. The sign is on her table under a tin cup. Stroud's real warning is on the inside of her door. The coffee can is on the shelf. Owen's page is in the Bible, and she will not show it until she has decided the party is not anyone's hired men, including hers. What earns it: kindness to Pete, honesty about who has offered them money, and a promise to find out the truth rather than a name. The scene's last beat is the burial plan for Wednesday on the bluff, and Thea's question: 'They say Owen gave up the claim. Did he? He never said.'
scenes.readAloud: The cabin is one room, swept, with a plank floor that Owen laid himself, a cookstove, a bed with a quilt, a table, a shelf of a dozen books, and the long shape on the bed under a sheet that nobody looks at. Thea Lasker gives you coffee because that is what you do, and sits with her hands round her own cup and does not drink it. 'The sign's there,' she says, nodding at the table, where a square of heavy paper lies face down under a tin cup. 'I couldn't leave it on him. I'll want it back.' Then she says, not looking at you, 'I heard horses, Sunday night, late. Two, maybe. Owen went out. Somebody called him about a cow in the creek. I thought it was the Company's riders and I was afraid, and I stayed in. I stayed in.' She puts the cup down. 'Ask what you want.'

skillChecks.success: She is hiding something, and she keeps glancing at the shelf where the family Bible is. She is afraid not of you but of someone she knows. If you tell her honestly who you work for and what you mean to do, she takes the Bible down and shows you Owen's page (CLUE C4).
skillChecks.failure: She is a grieving woman holding herself together. You do not see what else she is holding.

skillChecks.success: Owen's wrists have rope burns: they were tied in front, with the same rope, and he fought. There is a bruise on his temple from a pistol barrel. He was taken at gunpoint by at least two men. Nothing about it says the Association, whose two known killings in other valleys were rifle shots from cover.
skillChecks.failure: You can see how he died; you would rather not look closer. Dr. Haskell will at the inquest.

skillChecks.success: On the inside of the door, half hidden by a hanging coat: a square of cartridge-box card nailed up, pencil capitals, LASKER YOU ARE WARND OUT. 30 DAYS. P.R.S.G.A. 5 APRIL (CLUE A2). Thea moved it there so Pete would not read it. 'He laughed at it,' she says. 'He said Stroud could count to thirty.'
skillChecks.failure: You notice the coffee can on the shelf above the stove, and that Thea's eyes go to it whenever money is mentioned.

encounters: The street brawl (two Saloon Brawlers and one Drunk Cowboy against three homesteaders), brawling rules, nobody meant to die
Nils Solberg and three young homesteaders (use Rustler stats, armed with carbines) who mean to ride on the Forks unless talked down or stopped

acts.title: Tuesday to Thursday: The Inquest, the Notary and the Funeral
acts.description: The law does its little, the town talks, and the evidence is in the street for anyone who walks it. Dr. Abigail Haskell, acting coroner, holds the inquest on Tuesday morning; the six-man jury, three Company men and three grangers picked by the sheriff to offend nobody, returns 'death by hanging at the hands of persons unknown' before lunch. Gideon Sayre helpfully shows the relinquishment and, on Tuesday afternoon, records Elam Henley's entry. Greaves, the smith and Kemble's slate each hold a clue. Owen is buried on Wednesday on the bluff above the Narrows, and the funeral turns into a political meeting. On Thursday Sayre mails the papers to Cheyenne on the stage. A party that is quick can have the drifters' names by Tuesday night; a party that tells the wrong person will find Henley and Pettit gone to 'look for work at the roundup' by Wednesday.
objectives: Attend the inquest and get Dr. Haskell's findings
Follow the bar shoe, the rope and the money to Henley and Pettit
Notice the paper and the handwriting, and wonder about the notary
Speak at, or keep the peace at, Owen Lasker's funeral

scenes.name: Persons Unknown
scenes.description: The inquest in the courthouse's commissioners' room, Tuesday at nine, Dr. Abigail Haskell presiding. She is careful, dry and fearless and wants the truth on the record even though the jury will not give it. She will call any party member who found something at the Narrows as a witness. Sheriff Quinlan wants it over by noon. The room is packed and divided. If the party testifies to the tracks, the sign's paper and Stroud's card, the jury still returns 'persons unknown', because three of them ride for the Company and three are afraid, but the testimony is in Lavinia Thorpe's notebook and in Saturday's Plainsman, and Gideon Sayre hears it from the back of the room.
scenes.readAloud: The commissioners' room smells of new pine, wet wool and tobacco. Six jurymen sit along one wall on a bench, three in big hats and three in their Sunday coats, none of them looking at the others. At the table, in a black dress and steel spectacles, with a coroner's book open in front of her, a woman of about fifty with grey hair pulled back hard and a face like a well-kept tool. 'I am Abigail Haskell,' she says, 'physician, and acting coroner of Ransom County, because nobody else in it can write the word. We are here to determine how Owen Lasker died and, if we can, by whose hand. I will have no speeches and no spitting.' At the back, by the door, a neat man in a grey suit takes off his hat and stands quietly, as if he were in church.

skillChecks.success: Your testimony lands. The jury still returns persons unknown, but Dr. Haskell adds a rider in her own hand: 'The jury notes evidence that the deceased was taken by two riders who came from and returned toward Gilead.' Lavinia Thorpe writes it down. Reputation +1 for speaking plainly in public.
skillChecks.failure: The sheriff cuts you off as 'speculation', the jury returns persons unknown in four minutes, and someone on the Company side laughs.

skillChecks.success: The neat man at the back, Gideon Sayre, the notary, goes very still when anyone mentions the sign's paper, then smiles and nods sympathetically at the widow. He leaves before the verdict.
skillChecks.failure: The room is full of people with something to hide. You cannot pick one.

skillChecks.success: Dr. Haskell's findings, which she will share with any party member who asks after: death by strangulation, not a drop; hands tied in front; a pistol-barrel bruise; and fibres of new manila in the wrist burns. 'Two men at least. Men who had never done it before, God help them, or they would have done it quicker.'
skillChecks.failure: The medical evidence is read in Latin and the jury does not understand it; you do not either.

scenes.name: The Notary's Kindness
scenes.description: Gideon Sayre's office. However the party comes here, to look at the plat map, to ask who owned what, or because they are following the paper, Sayre is the most helpful man in Gilead. He offers coffee, a chair and his sincere opinion that 'Ballantine and his hired gunmen have gone too far this time'. He volunteers the forged relinquishment, sorrowfully, as proof that Owen 'meant to give up and go back to Iowa'. On Tuesday afternoon, while the party is there or just after, Elam Henley comes in to file on the Narrows. Run this as a quiet, creepy scene: the villain in plain sight, being kind. The party should leave feeling that something is wrong and not able to say what, unless they compare the sign's lettering with Sayre's register on the counter.
scenes.readAloud: Gideon Sayre's office is the neatest room in Ransom County. A big plat map of the valley fills one wall, every quarter-section squared off and pencilled with a name, the creek a blue thread through the middle. Pigeonholes of printed forms. A roll-top desk with every pen in its place. Sayre himself is a slim, grey, handsome man of about fifty with gold spectacles, ink on the second finger of his right hand, and the gentlest voice in Wyoming. 'You'll be the people the widow has asked to help her,' he says, coming round the counter to shake hands. 'God bless you for it. Sit down. There's coffee. Anything I have is at your service: the maps, the filings, all of it. I was the grange's secretary before there was a grange. Owen was a friend of mine.'

skillChecks.success: Sayre's hand in his register, the capitals especially, the looped R and the long-tailed G, is the hand on the sign; the ink is the same black iron-gall. And the blank forms in his pigeonholes are the same printed Land Office paper as the sign's back (CLUE C1). He sees you looking, and smiles.
skillChecks.failure: A careful clerk's office, full of careful clerk's handwriting. It all looks alike to you.

skillChecks.success: He is telling you about the relinquishment because he needs you to repeat it. He is waiting to see if you will. He is also very interested in where you have been and what you found at the Narrows.
skillChecks.failure: A kind man in a hard week. If anything, he seems the one person in town who is on everybody's side.

skillChecks.success: You let him think you believe it was Stroud. Sayre relaxes, and tells you, 'between ourselves', that Stroud was seen on the creek road on Saturday. (True: he was nailing his card on Calvin Booker's door.) He does not warn Henley and Pettit, who stay in town until Friday.
skillChecks.failure: He sees through you, and smiles, and by Wednesday Henley and Pettit have ridden out 'to look for roundup work'. Sayre writes to the Association that 'strangers are meddling'.

scenes.name: On the Bluff
scenes.description: Wednesday, the funeral on the bluff above the Narrows: a pine box, a hundred people, the grange's banner and, at a distance on the ridge, three Company riders sitting their horses and watching. Gustav Lindahl, if he is played, preaches; otherwise the Methodist circuit rider has not come and someone must. Margit Solberg speaks for the grange; Gideon Sayre speaks after her, movingly, for 'standing together', and calls for the grange to arm and to send to Cheyenne, which is what he wants. Nils Solberg wants to ride up to the three watchers on the ridge. The scene is about the community and the party's place in it: who speaks, who keeps the peace, who is seen standing with whom.
scenes.readAloud: They bury Owen Lasker on the bluff above the Narrows, where you can see the creek, the ford, the cottonwood and twenty miles of valley going green in the sun. The box is pine, planed by a neighbour in the night. There are a hundred people: every homestead on the creek and some from Gilead, women in black and men in their good coats with gun belts under them, children who have been told to be quiet, a grange banner, blue and gold, snapping in the wind. The widow stands at the head of the grave with the boy, and does not cry. A quarter of a mile away on the opposite ridge, against the sky, three riders sit their horses and watch, and do not take their hats off.

skillChecks.success: If you speak at the grave, you find words the valley remembers. Reputation +1, and whichever side you are working for, the other side hears that you spoke well of a dead man. A Preacher may use Fire and Brimstone here to steady the mourners.
skillChecks.failure: Your words are lost in the wind. Gideon Sayre's are not: he calls for the grange to arm, and the crowd roars.

skillChecks.success: You ride out to the three Company riders on the ridge (or signal them) and make it clear that this is a funeral. They take their hats off, and ride away. The grange sees it; so does Tolliver, when he hears.
skillChecks.failure: The riders stay where they are. Nils Solberg starts toward his horse, and you will have to stop him by hand.

skillChecks.success: Ira Pettit is at the funeral, at the very back, hat in his hands, and he leaves before the box goes in. Elam Henley is not. Pettit's horse is tied by the road, and it is shaking as badly as he is.
skillChecks.failure: A hundred faces. You do not pick out the one that matters.

encounters: No set combat. If the party confronts Henley and Pettit in town before Friday, Henley (use Outlaw) draws; Pettit (use Rustler) runs. A gunfight on Main Street is a Reputation matter: who drew first, who was armed, who was watching
The three Company riders on the ridge (Hired Guns, if it comes to that; it should not)

acts.title: Friday and Saturday: The Guns Arrive
acts.description: The war arrives on the Rawlins stage. On Friday eight hired gunmen from Cheyenne, with Association stock inspectors' commissions, step down outside the Ransom House, and Jubal Stroud rides in to meet them. On the way he has nailed thirty-day cards on Nils Solberg's door and Fergus Mallory's empty cabin; Calvin Booker's went up the Saturday before the hanging. Lavinia Thorpe has the dead list and must decide whether to print it in Saturday's Plainsman. Cyrus Ballantine rides to the Narrows on Saturday morning to offer Thea $300. On Saturday night the grange meets at Solberg's Bend to vote on arming. This act is where the party first meets Stroud and can hear from his own mouth why the hanging was not his work, and where they decide what to do with what they know: tell the grange, tell the sheriff, tell the Plainsman, tell their employer, or keep it.
objectives: Meet Jubal Stroud and take his measure without starting a fight you cannot finish
Help Lavinia Thorpe decide whether to print the dead list
Be present when Ballantine makes his offer to the widow
Attend the grange meeting, and decide what to tell it

scenes.name: The Friday Stage
scenes.description: Friday, four in the afternoon, outside the Ransom House: the Rawlins stage pulls in and eight men get down, in long coats, with rifle cases and carpet bags, and Association commissions in their pockets. Jubal Stroud rides in to meet them. This is the party's first sight of Stroud. He is not a brute: a lean, quiet, clean man of forty in a grey coat, with a soft voice, a good horse and a professional's interest in other armed people. He will speak to the party if they speak to him, with cold courtesy. If anyone accuses him of the hanging, he is offended, not frightened, and says exactly why it was not his work (CLUE A5). If anyone insults him in front of the street, he offers a showdown for the next morning, and means it; at level 2 or 3 this is suicide, and the party should be allowed to find a way out with their lives and the loss of a point of Reputation, or with wit.
scenes.readAloud: The Rawlins stage comes in behind six lathered horses and a horn you can hear from the bridge, and before it has stopped rocking the doors open and men get down, one after another: eight of them, in long dusters with the dust of two days on them, with carpet bags and leather rifle cases and the way of standing that men have when they are paid to be looked at. The street goes quiet. Across it, a rider on a tall grey horse walks it slowly up to the hotel rail, and dismounts, and the eight men straighten. He is lean and tidy and quiet, in a grey coat with a clean collar, a man you would take for a stock buyer or a dentist except for the ivory-handled revolver worn low, and his eyes. They go over the street once, the sheriff, the grangers outside Greaves, the Company boys at the Antelope, you, and they stay on you for exactly as long as it takes to count you. Then he touches his hat.

skillChecks.success: Stroud is vain about his work and his rules, and genuinely contemptuous of the hanging: 'I give thirty days. I nail a card. Then I come with paper or I come with a rifle. I have never hanged a man in my life and I don't use signs like a schoolboy.' He means it (CLUE A5). He also means every word of what follows: 'Anyone else on my list has his thirty days, same as Lasker had. Then I come.'
skillChecks.failure: A cold man saying what a cold man would say. You cannot tell if it is true.

skillChecks.success: In a stare-down with Stroud, you hold his eyes and he is the one who looks away first, with a small smile. He does not back down, but he remembers you, and from now on he treats you as someone worth a fair fight, which is the most dangerous compliment in Wyoming.
skillChecks.failure: You look away first. If this was a challenge, you may now back down with your life and lose a point of Reputation, or face him at sunup.

skillChecks.success: In the Antelope that night, over cards with two of the Association gunmen, you learn they are paid $5 a day and $50 'for every rustler killed or brought in', the Association's commissions are real, and they have been told the work will start 'after the roundup, when the papers come from Rawlins' (a first hint of CLUE D3).
skillChecks.failure: They play close and drink little and lose politely. Professionals.

scenes.name: Three Hundred Dollars
scenes.description: Saturday morning at the Narrows: Cyrus Ballantine rides down from the Forks with Wade Tolliver and two riders, and in the widow's cabin offers Thea Lasker $300 cash for the Narrows claim and its improvements, 'out of sympathy, and so you can go home'. He is courteous, cold and sincere about the money; he cannot imagine a woman alone keeping a claim. Thea refuses. If the party is present, this is their chance to see Ballantine and Tolliver side by side, and to see Tolliver's discomfort. If the party has told anyone about Owen's relinquishment, Ballantine mentions it ('I'm told he had already given it up; then my offer is generous'), which tells the party how fast Sayre's story is spreading.
scenes.readAloud: Ballantine sits at the widow's table with his hat on his knee and his gloves in his hat, a straight grey man in a black coat, with a short white beard and a voice from Edinburgh that has been in Laramie long enough to say 'claim' like a local. Behind him in the doorway, ducking under the lintel, is a big weathered man in a sheepskin coat who looks at the floor. Ballantine lays three hundred-dollar notes on the table, one beside the other. 'Mrs. Lasker. I'm sorry for your loss, and I'm a practical man, and I'll be practical. This is a hard country for a woman alone. Here is three hundred dollars for the claim and the improvements. You can be on the Rawlins stage on Tuesday, and home in Iowa by the end of the month.'

skillChecks.success: Ballantine is not lying: he did not order Owen hanged, and he has no idea who did, and he does not much care. The big man in the doorway, Wade Tolliver, cares a great deal; he is ashamed to be here.
skillChecks.failure: A rich man buying a dead man's land. You cannot see past that, and maybe there is nothing past it.

skillChecks.success: Outside, by the horses, Tolliver talks to you, low: he fired two drunks in February, Henley and Pettit; Henley rides a bay with a bar shoe; and he will not be party to hanging men or to burning out women. 'You tell that to anyone, I'll call you a liar.' (A step toward turning Tolliver in bk-scenario-002.)
skillChecks.failure: Tolliver says nothing and rides away behind his boss.

skillChecks.success: You make it clear to Ballantine, politely, that the widow is under your protection. He picks up his notes, unoffended, and says, 'Then you'll be on the other side, I suppose. I'm sorry for it.' The Company's attitude drops a step, and the grange's rises.
skillChecks.failure: Ballantine looks at you as at a hired man speaking out of turn, and leaves the notes on the table for a minute longer than he needs to.

scenes.name: The Grange Meets
scenes.description: Saturday night, the log grange hall at Solberg's Bend: sixty people, lanterns, a pot-bellied stove, the blue and gold banner, coffee and pie. Margit Solberg presides with a gavel. The motion is to arm, to post night riders, and to send Margit to Cheyenne to petition the governor. Gideon Sayre, the secretary, takes the minutes and speaks hardest for arming. Calvin Booker, with Stroud's card in his pocket, speaks against riding on the Forks: 'They want us to come to them.' Lavinia Thorpe is there with the dead list in her bag and has not decided. Whatever the party knows, this is where they decide whether to say it, and to whom. Telling the hall that Henley and Pettit did the hanging now, without proof the judge will accept, sends Nils Solberg and twenty men to find them tonight, and the drifters will be hanged by morning if they are found: a second lynching, and a crime. Telling Margit privately is safer. Telling Sayre is the worst thing they can do, and the most natural.
scenes.readAloud: The grange hall is a long log building that smells of lamp oil, coffee and wet coats, and it is fuller than it has ever been. Sixty people on benches, children asleep on coats along the back wall, a pot-bellied stove glowing red, and over the platform the grange's banner, blue silk with a gold sheaf of wheat. Margit Solberg raps the gavel. Beside her, at a little table with the minute book open and a pen in his hand, Gideon Sayre looks up at you and nods kindly. 'The question before the grange,' says Margit, in her careful English, 'is whether we arm ourselves, and post riders at night, and whether I go to Cheyenne to see the governor. Owen Lasker was my neighbour. Speak, if you have something to say, and then we vote.'

skillChecks.success: You carry the room: the grange votes to arm for defence only, to post night riders, and not to ride on the Forks. Nils Solberg sits down. Margit goes to Cheyenne. Reputation +1 with the grange's people; Sayre writes it all in the minutes and looks at you thoughtfully.
skillChecks.failure: Sayre carries the room. The grange votes to arm and to 'answer any outrage in kind'. That vote is the excuse Ballantine will use in May.

skillChecks.success: Watching the room: Sayre is pushing for a fight while appearing to counsel restraint; every time Calvin Booker says 'they want us to come to them', Sayre speaks next. And Lavinia Thorpe keeps her hand on her bag.
skillChecks.failure: Everyone is frightened and everyone is angry. Nobody stands out.

skillChecks.success: You keep what you know about Henley and Pettit out of the hall without lying to Margit, and tell her later, alone, by the stove. She listens, goes white, and says, 'Then I will not let them hang. We are not the Company.' She will help keep the secret until there is proof.
skillChecks.failure: Someone hears. By morning the story is all over the creek that 'the strangers know who did it', and Sayre knows it too.

encounters: Jubal Stroud (use Fast Gun) and eight hired gunmen from the Association (use Hired Gun): no fight is meant here; a showdown with Stroud at level 2 or 3 should be survivable only by not drawing
If the party has driven Henley and Pettit to bolt, they are caught on the Rawlins road by Saturday (Henley: Outlaw; Pettit: Rustler), and whether they reach a cell alive is the party's choice

npcsInvolved.name: Thea Lasker, 27
npcsInvolved.role: The widow; the party's possible employer; the claim's rightful holder
npcsInvolved.description: Thin, fair, brown-eyed, in a man's coat over a black dress, a schoolteacher's daughter from Iowa who married a dreamer with a claim. Steady, proud, frightened, and much harder than she looks. Has a six-year-old son, Pete. Has $112 in a coffee can and a page in the family Bible.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To know who killed Owen and why, and to keep the Narrows for Pete. She does not want revenge; she wants the truth and the claim.

npcsInvolved.name: Gideon Sayre, 49
npcsInvolved.role: Land locator, notary public, U.S. Commissioner and grange secretary; the man who ordered the hanging
npcsInvolved.description: Slim, grey, handsome, gold spectacles, ink on his finger, the gentlest voice in Wyoming. Came out in 1879 from Ohio after a bank failure nobody here knows about. The most helpful man in Ransom County.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Money and safety. He wants the Narrows sold to the railroad, the war to empty the creek, and nobody ever to know that he sold his neighbours' names to the Association.

npcsInvolved.name: Elam Henley, 34
npcsInvolved.role: Drifter, ex-BC rider; one of the hangmen; the entryman on the Narrows
npcsInvolved.description: Long, lantern-jawed, quick to grin, quick to hit, a good rider and a mean drunk, on a bay gelding with a bar shoe on the near fore. Has a new Army revolver.
npcsInvolved.motivation: His $200, the Narrows paper, and to never think about Sunday night.

npcsInvolved.name: Ira Pettit, 20
npcsInvolved.role: Drifter, ex-BC rider; the other hangman; bought the rope
npcsInvolved.description: Thin, freckled, a boy from Nebraska who wanted to be a cowboy and became a drunk's sidekick. Has not slept since Sunday.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To undo it. He cannot. Next best: to tell someone, and not to be hanged for it.

npcsInvolved.name: Cyrus Ballantine, 51
npcsInvolved.role: Manager of the Bitter Creek Land & Cattle Company
npcsInvolved.description: Straight, grey, short white beard, Edinburgh by way of Laramie, a black coat and a gold watch. Never raises his voice and never forgets a debt.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To return a dividend to his investors, which means clearing the creek of homesteaders and getting the Narrows before the railroad comes.

npcsInvolved.name: Wade Tolliver, 46
npcsInvolved.description: Big, weathered, sheepskin coat, a Texas cowman who came up the trail in 1874 and stayed. Hard, fair by his lights, a man of his word, sick of the way things are going.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To run the roundup, keep his men alive, and not be part of anything he would be ashamed to tell his nephew. Can be turned.

npcsInvolved.name: Jubal Stroud, 40
npcsInvolved.role: The Association's range detective on the Company's payroll
npcsInvolved.description: Lean, tidy, quiet, grey coat, clean collar, an ivory-handled Army revolver worn low, a Sharps buffalo rifle in a saddle scabbard. Speaks softly. Has killed men in two other valleys.
npcsInvolved.motivation: His fee, his reputation and his rules: thirty days, then paper or a rifle. Insulted to be blamed for a hanging.

npcsInvolved.name: Margit Solberg, 52
npcsInvolved.role: Worthy Master of Bitter Creek Grange No. 9
npcsInvolved.description: Grey-haired, broad, strong-handed, a Norwegian widow who came out in 1879 and proved up two claims. Speaks careful English and thinks before every word.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To keep the grange together, keep her son Nils alive, and keep the creek.

npcsInvolved.name: Sheriff Silas Quinlan, 55
npcsInvolved.role: Sheriff of Ransom County; the man who owes everyone
npcsInvolved.description: Stout, grey, kindly, tired, badge pinned crooked. Elected with Company money and grange votes; owes Beau Fairchild $400 at cards.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To get through the summer without having to choose. He will choose, if pushed, and he would rather be pushed by someone he respects.

npcsInvolved.name: Lavinia Thorpe, 40
npcsInvolved.role: Editor and owner of the Gilead Plainsman
npcsInvolved.description: Small, quick, ink-stained, a widow who sets type faster than her late husband did. Prints the Company's advertisements and the grange's notices and her own opinions.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To print the truth and keep the paper alive, which in Ransom County are not the same thing.

npcsInvolved.name: Dr. Abigail Haskell (companion)
npcsInvolved.description: See her companion sheet. Presides at the inquest and can read the body.

npcsInvolved.name: Otis Greaves and Moses Kearney
npcsInvolved.description: Greaves: bald, anxious, a ledger man. Kearney: huge, slow, burned forearms, remembers every hoof in the county.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To get paid, and to stay out of the war.

rewards.money: Whoever hired the party pays: the Company $60 a head for the month (Association commissions included), the grange $20 a head and loaned horses, the sheriff $3 a day each in cash or scrip, or Thea Lasker's $112, which a decent party will try to give back. A party that settles the street brawl may be stood drinks; anything taken from Henley if he is caught (about $70 in new notes) is evidence.
items: The sign (CLUE A1), on Land Office paper, if Thea lends it to the party
Owen's notebook page, 'G.S. is the one giving names' (CLUE C4), if Thea trusts them
Owen's draft letter to the railroad's chief engineer and Ballantine's February offer (CLUES E2, E3)
Dr. Haskell's coroner's findings, written out, if she was asked
A copy of the Plainsman of Saturday 24 April, with or without the dead list

twists: Gideon Sayre is the most helpful man the party meets this week, and he will be helpful throughout the campaign. He offers maps, introductions, the township records, his opinion that the Company did it, and later his services as notary for any paper the party needs. Every helpful thing he does is also a way of finding out what they know. If they tell him who did the hanging, Henley and Pettit leave town the next morning, and Sayre writes to Cheyenne about 'meddling strangers'.

The relinquishment Sayre shows the party is dated 10 April and says Owen gave up the claim. Thea knows Owen never would have. She cannot prove it yet; the proof is in the railroad survey party's payroll book, forty miles away in the foothills, which arrives on the Sage Flats in May (bk-scenario-002).

Lavinia Thorpe's anonymous copy of the dead list was mailed from Cheyenne by the Association's own clerk, who has a conscience. If she prints it on Saturday, the nine living men on it know, the valley is outraged, the Association recalls nobody and Ballantine moves the raid forward by a week; if she does not, the men on it find out one card at a time.

The party may want to hand Henley and Pettit to the sheriff on Tuesday. They can. Quinlan will hold them, the justice of the peace will release them on Thursday for lack of evidence (a rope purchase and a horseshoe are not a hanging), and the grange will know where they are for two days. Every night of those two days, someone has to stand in front of the jail.
dmTips: This scenario establishes the valley, the factions and the mystery. Budget an hour for Monday, an hour and a half for Tuesday to Thursday, and an hour for Friday and Saturday. The only expected fights are the street brawl and possibly Nils Solberg's friends; the party can avoid both.

Let the players choose an employer and make the choice matter. A party on the Company's payroll can ride to the Narrows as the Company's eyes, and find the same clues; the drama is in what they tell Ballantine. A party on the grange's side meets Stroud as an enemy. A party working for Thea has the most freedom and the least money.

The sign is the key. Describe it carefully the first time anyone picks it up: heavy printed paper, the back lettered in a clerk's beautiful hand. Then, whenever they meet Gideon Sayre, describe his handwriting the same way, in the same words, and let them notice.

Do not let the party solve the whole mystery this week. They should end it knowing (A) that the Association did not do it and (B) that Henley and Pettit did, with a thread toward Sayre. If they leap straight to Sayre, let them: he is a federal officer, the grange's secretary and the most respected man on the creek; nobody will believe them without the forged relinquishment proved false, which needs the survey payroll in bk-scenario-002.

Stroud is a Fast Gun at CR 5 and the party is level 2. If a player calls him out, run the stare-down honestly and let the loser back down with their life. Stroud does not kill people who back down; he lets them live with it. That is worse, and it costs a point of Reputation.

Lynching is a horror, not a solution. If the grange learns about Henley and Pettit too early and goes to hang them, play the mob scene with full weight and make the party choose whether to stand in front of the jail.
Use Reputation from the first scene. Announce the starting score (0) and every change. The town is watching the strangers.

End the scenario with two Plainsman headlines for the 24 April edition: what Lavinia printed about the inquest, and whether she printed the dead list. Then summarise the two weeks until the roundup: Margit in Cheyenne, Stroud's cards, the creek greening, and the date coming.
